topic: Fundamentals of Linear Algebra: Vectors as Arrows
target_audience: High school students and introductory computer science learners

outline.topic: Fundamentals of Linear Algebra: Vectors as Arrows
outline.target_audience: High school students and introductory computer science learners

sections.title: Introduction: What is a Vector?
sections.content: Define a vector not just as a list of numbers, but as a directed segment in 2D space. Explain the 'origin' and 'tip' to help visualize movement.
sections.example: Visualize a robotic arm at the origin (0,0) reaching out to a coordinate (3,2). The vector is the arrow connecting the start to the target.

sections.title: Vector Addition: The Head-to-Tail Rule
sections.content: Introduce vector addition geometrically. Explain that adding two vectors is equivalent to 'walking' the first path, then starting the second path from the end of the first.
sections.example: A cat walks 2 steps East and 3 steps North. Then, it walks another 1 step East and 1 step North. Use a coordinate grid to show the resulting final position (3,4).

sections.title: Scalar Multiplication: Stretching and Flipping
sections.content: Explain how multiplying a vector by a constant (scalar) changes its length. Discuss how negative scalars flip the direction entirely.
sections.example: A video game character jumping: A vector represents the jump strength. Doubling the vector (scalar 2) makes the character jump twice as high; multiplying by -1 makes the character jump downwards.

sections.title: Basis Vectors: The Building Blocks
sections.content: Introduce 'i-hat' (1,0) and 'j-hat' (0,1) as the fundamental basis. Explain that every vector is just a scaled combination of these two pillars.
sections.example: Using Lego bricks: Think of 'i-hat' as a red brick and 'j-hat' as a blue brick. Any coordinate (x, y) is simply x red bricks and y blue bricks stacked together.

sections.title: Summary and Conclusion
sections.content: Synthesize the concepts: Vectors are movements, addition is combining paths, scalars are scaling, and basis vectors are the coordinate system's DNA.
sections.example: Briefly show a navigation app on a phone: '2 miles North, 1 mile East' is effectively a vector addition problem used in real-time GPS tracking.

storyboard.title: Introduction: What is a Vector?
lecture_lines: Vectors are arrows, not just lists of numbers.
Think of an arrow from origin to (3, 2).
The starting point is always the origin.
The tip shows the destination point clearly.
This arrow defines a specific movement in space.
animations: Display a single point in 2D space #FFFFFF.
Draw an arrow from the origin to the point.
Label the arrow as vector 'v' in color #FF00FF.
Show the x-coordinate and y-coordinate components separately.
Highlight the arrow again to reinforce the vector concept.

storyboard.title: Vector Addition: The Head-to-Tail Rule
lecture_lines: Vector addition combines two distinct movements together.
Walk the first path, then the second path.
Start the second path at the first's tip.
Example: 2 East, 3 North, then 1 East, 1 North.
The result is a new vector: (3, 4).
animations: Display two vectors 'v' and 'w' in color #00FFFF.
Move vector 'w' so its tail meets the head of 'v'.
Draw a new vector from the origin to the new head.

storyboard.title: Scalar Multiplication: Stretching and Flipping
lecture_lines: Scalar multiplication stretches or flips a vector's length.
A scalar of two doubles the vector length.
Negative scalars flip the vector's direction completely.
Example: Jump twice as high with scalar two.
Multiply by negative one to reverse the jump.
animations: Scale 'v' by a factor of 2 to show stretching.
Scale 'v' by -1 to show flipping direction.

storyboard.title: Basis Vectors: The Building Blocks
lecture_lines: Basis vectors are fundamental building blocks of space.
We call these units i-hat and j-hat.
Every vector is a combination of these pillars.
Imagine i-hat as a horizontal red brick.
J-hat is like a vertical blue brick.
animations: Show grid lines to define the coordinate space.
Animate a vector expressed as a linear combination of 'i' and 'j'.

storyboard.title: Summary and Conclusion
lecture_lines: Vectors represent motion; addition combines these paths.
Scalars scale motion; basis vectors define our coordinates.
Think of GPS: adding vectors for precise navigation.
animations: Fade in summary text of vector operations in #FFFFFF.
Flash the key formulas for addition and scalar multiplication.
Fade out all elements to black.
